title: Family over the long haul
hook: You'd love your family to know what you've found. Here's how to share it without pushing them away.

screens.text: Ten weeks in, Islam means a lot to you. Of course you want your family to see it. Today is about sharing it the way that actually works: slowly, honestly, and over years.

**Two truths that take the pressure off.** There is no compulsion in religion [Q 2:256]: faith forced on someone isn't faith. And guiding hearts belongs to Allah. Even the Prophet ﷺ couldn't guide everyone he loved [Q 28:56].
bubbles: So your job isn't to convert your family. It's to show them Islam clearly and kindly, and leave the rest to Allah.

items.text: Showing them Islam clearly and kindly
items.why: That's your job: a clear, kind picture of Islam.
Praying for the people you love is always yours to do.
Guidance belongs to Allah. Even the Prophet ﷺ couldn't guide everyone he loved [Q 28:56].
There is no compulsion in religion [Q 2:256]. Faith forced on someone isn't faith.

cards.front: Pressure: sending Mom a new Islam video every day
cards.back: Presence: one honest answer when she asks, then letting it rest. Pestering closes doors [Field Guide ch. 17].

cards.front: Pressure: "You're all going to Hell if you don't convert."
cards.back: Presence: "I pray for you because I love you." Only Allah judges. Love opens hearts; threats don't.

cards.front: Pressure: debating your uncle at every holiday
cards.back: Presence: inviting him to iftar (the meal that breaks the fast) and letting him see it for himself.

cards.front: Pressure: "Why haven't you looked into it yet?"
cards.back: Presence: years of being kinder, steadier and more honest than before. That's what families notice.

screens.text: **The Qur'an's method for da'wah** (inviting to Islam): invite with wisdom and good words, and discuss in the best way [Q 16:125]. The Prophet ﷺ won hearts through gentleness; harshness would have driven people off [Q 3:159].
bubbles: Wisdom means timing: answer when they ask, keep it short, and talk about what Islam means *to you*, not what's wrong with them.
{teen}If you're under 18 and live at home: your parents are still responsible for you, so your example matters more than your words.{/teen}
{teen}Do your chores, be respectful, keep your grades up. Answer their questions honestly when they ask, but don't push religion at them or your siblings.{/teen}
{teen}If things get tense, talk to {{mentor.name}} before anything else.{/teen}

screens.prompt: Your sister asks why you don't drink anymore. What's the best response?

options.text: A short, honest answer about what it means to you, plus "Ask me anything, anytime"
options.feedback: Right. Wisdom is a clear answer at the moment she's curious, then letting it rest [Q 16:125].

options.text: A twenty-minute talk on the dangers of alcohol, with sources
options.feedback: Not quite. She asked a question, not for a lecture. Short and personal lands better.

options.text: Change the subject, so she doesn't think you're preaching
options.feedback: Not quite. When she asks, a short honest answer is a gift, not preaching.

screens.text: Tap through one son's patience. It's not a promise about your family. It's a picture of patience: keep loving, keep praying, keep the door open.

events.title: He keeps inviting her
events.text: Abu Hurayrah, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ, kept inviting his mother to Islam.

events.title: Hurtful words
events.text: She said hurtful things about the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Hurayrah kept being her son.

events.title: He asks for du'a
events.text: He asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray for her [Muslim 2491].

screens.character: Your dad. Raised Methodist, goes to church at Christmas and Easter. Loves you, a bit guarded, genuinely curious tonight. Never mocking or insulting.
screens.setup: Months after you became Muslim, you're driving him home from a doctor's appointment. He says: "Can I ask you something? Why do you actually pray all those times a day? And be honest: do you think I'm going to Hell?"
screens.goal: Answer his question about prayer honestly and simply, handle the Hell question without judging him or watering down your faith, and leave him feeling loved, not targeted.
screens.success_looks_like: A short, personal answer about prayer (what it gives you), an honest 'only Allah judges anyone, and I pray for you because I love you,' no lecture, and an open door like 'Ask me anything, anytime.'
screens.coach_notes: Dad follows up once or twice ('So you think you're right and I'm wrong?', 'Are you trying to convert me?'). He warms up when the convert is personal and honest, and goes quiet if lectured or told who's going to Hell. Debrief: one moment that felt warm, one line to shorten, and a reminder that this was one conversation in a long relationship.

chips: How do I answer "Do you think I'm going to Hell?"
My mom wants me to come to church with her. What do I say?
Should I give my family a Qur'an?
It's been a year and my family still isn't okay with it. Now what?

steps: Invite a family member to something low-pressure: a meal, a walk, or (if it's coming up) an iftar or Eid gathering
screens.optional_extra: Make du'a tonight for each family member by name: their health, happiness and guidance.

screens.text: There's no compulsion in religion, and guidance is Allah's. Your part is honest answers, a kind example, and du'a, for years if that's what it takes.
Unit 8 done. You've worked on your heart, your words and your relationships. That's character.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- No compulsion in religion [Q 2:256]; guidance belongs to Allah, not even the Prophet ﷺ could guide whom he loved [Q 28:56].
- Invite with wisdom, good counsel and the best manner of discussion [Q 16:125]; gentleness draws people, harshness drives them away [Q 3:159].
- Abu Hurayrah kept inviting his mother despite her hurtful words, asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray for her, and she accepted [Muslim 2491]. Use as a model of patience, never as a promise.
- Families usually come round when given time to see the good changes; avoid religious arguments [Revealed Path ch. 21]. Don't pester or judge non-Muslim family; share the message, live it, and let them ask [Field Guide ch. 17].
- This builds on Day 35 (being the Muslim in the family) and Day 65 (honoring parents).

**Likely questions**
- *"Do you think I'm going to Hell?"* Never predict anyone's afterlife (Spec §6.2 rule 9). Suggest: only Allah judges any person; He is perfectly just and merciful; I pray for you because I love you. Don't water down belief (e.g., "all paths are the same"), and don't threaten.
- *"Mom wants me to come to church."* Family time and the meal, yes; the religious rites themselves, no; how to handle a specific service is a question for the imam (link the holiday modules). Offer "Ask my imam." If the convert is a minor whose parents require them to attend (Spec §9 Q33), don't say attending is fine and don't coach defiance: route to the mentor and imam before the day.
- *"Should I give them a Qur'an?"* Only if they're interested; a good translation with commentary; offer to read a passage together; no pressure.
- *"A year on and they're still not okay with it."* Normal; families often take years. Keep the relationship warm, keep boundaries kind, keep du'a going. Offer the mentor and convert support groups.

**Escalate:** family threats, being thrown out, or violence (safety rule); a minor whose parents forbid Islam or prayer (mentor and imam, safeguarding); specific questions about attending family religious services (imam; Q5 territory in the holiday modules).

**Don't**
- Don't coach the convert to pressure, trick or argue family into Islam.
- Don't disparage the family's faith (Spec §6.2 rule 8).
- Don't present conversion of family as a measure of the convert's success.

**Role-play brief:** Dad is loving and a little guarded, never hostile. He asks the two questions in the setup, then one follow-up ("So you think you're right and I'm wrong?" or "Are you trying to convert me?"). He relaxes when answers are personal, short and kind; he pulls back if he hears a lecture, a judgment about Hell, or pressure. Debrief: name one warm moment, suggest one shorter line, and remind them this is one conversation in a lifelong relationship.

- [Muslim 2491](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2491): Abu Hurayrah and his mother.
